paper.title: Role of the penile microbiome in female sex partner risk of bacterial vaginosis and sexually transmitted infections: a narrative review.

problem.title: Bacteria on the penis linked to bacterial vaginosis are associated with higher risk of bacterial vaginosis and sexually transmitted infections in female sex partners, yet what counts as a healthy penile microbiome is undefined.
problem.summary: The penile microbiome can be dominated by skin bacteria or by anaerobic bacteria associated with bacterial vaginosis (BV), and is shaped by circumcision, condom use, antibiotics and the partner's vaginal microbiome. In the few studies examining both partners at once, specific bacteria are highly correlated and appear to pass in both directions, and BV-associated penile bacteria are linked to higher BV and STI risk in female partners. Early trials suggest treating men with antimicrobials reduces penile anaerobic bacteria and lowers female partners' risk of BV recurrence.
problem.affected_women: Female sex partners of men, who face BV recurrence and sexually transmitted infections linked to their partner's penile bacteria.

data_need.description: Data defining optimal and non-optimal penile microbiome states, and on how, how durably, and under what conditions bacteria are exchanged between penis and vagina.
data_need.why_it_matters: Without these data there is no basis for screening assays, for monitoring after treatment in men and their female partners, or for treatment and counselling guidelines that could prevent repeated BV and STIs in women.

gap_evidence.note: The review states that data are lacking on factors influencing penile-vaginal bacterial exchangeability, the durability of bacterial exchange, and the conditions under which exchange leads to increased risk of adverse outcomes in the index person or partner; optimal and non-optimal penile microbiomes have not been defined; assessment of penile microbiome composition and function across the life course is needed; association with intrinsic host factors such as genetics and endogenous hormones is lacking, and association with behavioural and lifestyle factors is limited.

dataset_source.note: Published couples-based and partner-treatment studies (e.g. Mehta et al.'s Kenyan penile-microbiome/incident-BV cohort; StepUp male partner BV treatment trial with penile microbiota sampling) provide partial evidence that penile anaerobes predict BV in female partners. They do NOT define optimal/non-optimal penile community state types, do not measure durability or directionality of bacterial exchange over time, do not cover the life course, and lack linkage to host genetics or endogenous hormones. Geographic coverage is narrow (mainly Kenya, Uganda, Australia, US). Because live search failed, this citation is from memory and the specific record should be confirmed via the PubMed query link before use.

verification.findings: Live web search was unavailable during this check (the search tool returned a usage-limit error on every attempt), so this answer rests on published literature I can name but could not re-verify today — treat it as provisional. Relevant work does exist and partially overlaps the gap: Mehta and colleagues' Kenyan couples cohort linked penile microbiota composition (notably anaerobes such as Sneathia, Prevotella, Dialister) to incident bacterial vaginosis in female partners, and Plummer/Vodstrcil and colleagues have characterised penile microbiota in men whose partners have BV, with the StepUp randomised trial (Melbourne) testing concurrent male-partner antimicrobial treatment and including penile microbiota sampling. None of these, to my knowledge, has produced a consensus definition of optimal versus non-optimal penile microbiome states, nor systematic data on durability of penile-vaginal bacterial exchange, life-course composition, or associations with host genetics and endogenous hormones.
